lead: A partial differential equation (PDE) links a function z(x,y) to its partial derivatives. Often we know a family of surfaces with free constants or free functions. Eliminating those free choices by differentiation gives the PDE that all members satisfy. This is how a model becomes an equation: the constants disappear, the relation remains. Engineers use it when a measured family of surfaces must be written as one differential law, and examiners use it to test whether you can differentiate cleanly and eliminate completely.
prereq: You need partial differentiation and the chain rule from first-year calculus; p and q are defined here, and 4.2 shows what to do with a formed PDE.

blocks.text: Let z be the dependent variable and x, y the independent variables. Write z = z(x,y). The two first partial derivatives get short names:

blocks.where: p is the x-derivative with y held fixed; q is the y-derivative with x held fixed. A first-order PDE contains x, y, z, p and q, but no second derivatives such as ∂²z/∂x².

blocks.text: The order is the highest derivative present. Formation asks only for the equation; solving it is a separate job.

Start with a relation F(x,y,z,a,b)=0, where a and b are arbitrary constants. Differentiate the relation with respect to x while y is fixed. Differentiate with respect to y while x is fixed. The two new equations contain a and b. Use them with the original relation to remove a and b.

items: Write the given relation as F(x,y,z,a,b)=0.
Differentiate with respect to x at fixed y; replace ∂z/∂x by p.
Differentiate with respect to y at fixed x; replace ∂z/∂y by q.
Eliminate a and b from the original relation and the two derivative equations.
The result, containing only x, y, z, p, q, is the first-order PDE.

blocks.text: If only one constant remains, one derivative equation plus the original relation is usually enough. A constant that appears together with another may still vanish in one step.

blocks.where: Φ is the formed PDE; a and b no longer appear. The arrow means elimination, not solving.

blocks.text: For one arbitrary function z = f(u), u = u(x,y), differentiate with respect to x and y by the chain rule. Let f′ be the derivative of f with respect to u.
p = f′(u) u<sub>x</sub>,  q = f′(u) u<sub>y</sub>
blocks.where: u<sub>x</sub> = ∂u/∂x, u<sub>y</sub> = ∂u/∂y, and f′ is d f / d u. The unknown function f′ appears in both equations.

blocks.text: Multiply the first equation by u<sub>y</sub> and the second by u<sub>x</sub>, then subtract. The f′ term cancels.

blocks.where: This is the first-order PDE for the family z = f(u). It contains u and its first derivatives, but not f itself.

blocks.text: For a relation F(u,v)=0, differentiate with respect to x and y. A nonzero pair F<sub>u</sub>, F<sub>v</sub> exists only if the determinant is zero.

blocks.where: This is the Jacobian condition ∂(u,v)/∂(x,y)=0. It is the first-order PDE for the family F(u,v)=0.

blocks.text: Two independent arbitrary functions, such as z=f(x)+g(y), normally give a second-order PDE; that belongs to Unit 5, not here.

figure.caption: The flow starts with the surface family, differentiates in x and y, substitutes p and q, and ends with the first-order PDE. Notice that the constants a and b do not survive.

spec.title: Forming a PDE from z = ax + by + ab
spec.aria: Flowchart shows differentiating z = ax + by + ab to get p = a and q = b, then substituting to form z = px + qy + pq.

examples.question: Form the partial differential equation by eliminating the arbitrary constants a and b from z = ax + by + ab.
steps: Given z = ax + by + ab, with a and b arbitrary constants.
Differentiate with respect to x at fixed y: ∂z/∂x = a, since by and ab are constant in x. So p = a.
Differentiate with respect to y at fixed x: ∂z/∂y = b, so q = b.
Substitute a = p and b = q into the original relation: z = p x + q y + p q.
The constants a and b are gone. The result contains x, y, z, p, q only, so it is first order.
examples.answer: The required PDE is z = px + qy + pq.

traps: Do not treat a and b as variables. They are constants, so ∂a/∂x = 0 and ∂b/∂y = 0.
Do not forget the chain rule in z = f(u). p = f′(u)u<sub>x</sub>, not just f′(u).
Do not mix the held-fixed variable. p is ∂z/∂x at fixed y; q is ∂z/∂y at fixed x.
Two arbitrary functions usually produce a second-order PDE. The first-order function formula applies to z=f(u) or F(u,v)=0.
Do not stop with a or b still present; elimination must be complete.

quiz.q: Define p and q for z(x,y), and state the order of a PDE that contains only p and q.
quiz.a: p = ∂z/∂x at fixed y, q = ∂z/∂y at fixed x. A PDE with only p and q, with no higher derivatives, is first order.

quiz.q: Why does differentiating a relation with arbitrary constants help form a PDE?
quiz.a: Differentiation gives equations that link the constants to p and q. Using these with the original relation lets us remove the constants and leave a relation between x, y, z, p and q.

quiz.q: Form the PDE by eliminating a and b from z = ax + by + a² + b².
quiz.a: p = a and q = b. Substitute into the original relation: z = px + qy + p² + q².

quiz.q: Form the PDE from z = f(x²+y²), where f is arbitrary.
quiz.a: Take u = x²+y². Then u<sub>x</sub> = 2x and u<sub>y</sub> = 2y. Use p u<sub>y</sub> − q u<sub>x</sub> = 0, so p(2y) − q(2x) = 0, giving yp − xq = 0.

quiz.q: For the family F(u,v)=0, derive the first-order PDE.
quiz.a: Differentiate F(u,v)=0 with respect to x and y: F<sub>u</sub>u<sub>x</sub>+F<sub>v</sub>v<sub>x</sub>=0 and F<sub>u</sub>u<sub>y</sub>+F<sub>v</sub>v<sub>y</sub>=0. A nonzero pair F<sub>u</sub>,F<sub>v</sub> exists only if u<sub>x</sub>v<sub>y</sub>−u<sub>y</sub>v<sub>x</sub>=0.

quiz.q: Form the PDE from z = ax + ay + a², where a is one arbitrary constant.
quiz.a: p = a and q = a. Eliminate a: p = q. The formed PDE is p = q.

quiz.q: Why does z=f(x)+g(y) give a second-order PDE, while z=f(u) gives a first-order PDE?
quiz.a: For z=f(x)+g(y), z<sub>x</sub>=f′(x) and z<sub>y</sub>=g′(y), so z<sub>xy</sub>=0, which is second order. For z=f(u), chain rule gives p and q sharing the single factor f′(u); eliminating f′ uses only first derivatives.

quiz.q: Write the PDE for the family z=f(u), naming p, q and u.
quiz.a: p u<sub>y</sub> − q u<sub>x</sub> = 0, where p=∂z/∂x, q=∂z/∂y, and u=u(x,y).

beyond: Not for the exam. Formation by elimination is the reverse of finding a complete integral. In geometric optics and Hamilton–Jacobi theory, families of wavefronts are encoded as first-order PDEs. In continuum mechanics, constitutive families become differential constraints. Search next for elimination of arbitrary functions PDE, Jacobian condition PDE, and complete integral.
